Females of the blue rockcod Indonotothenia cyanobrancha reach sexual maturity at a total length of 14 cm [Lp = 14 cm], a size that corresponds to a wet weight at puberty of approximately 67 grams [Wwp = approximately 67 grams]. This length-based threshold for reproductive onset is broadly comparable to values reported for other nototheniids from the Southern Ocean, although direct comparative data remain scarce. The relatively small size at maturation in this species likely reflects the energetic constraints imposed by the chronically cold, low-productivity waters of its high-latitude habitat. Growth trajectories derived from field-collected specimens indicate that females typically attain this pubertal size after several years of sustained somatic investment, with a total body length at puberty that is less than half the ultimate total length recorded for the species. The relationship between length and mass in these fish follows a standard power-law function, allowing reliable estimation of the mass at maturity from the more commonly measured length data.

Maximum recorded longevity in the blue rockcod is 18 years [am = 18 years], based on studies of the closely related nototheniid Notothenia coriiceps conducted at a stable water temperature of -1 °C [T = -1 °C]. This lifespan is notable among Antarctic teleosts, placing Indonotothenia cyanobrancha among the longer-lived members of its family. Otolith-based age estimates from wild-caught individuals confirm that senescence-related mortality begins to increase markedly only after the second decade of life, with very few individuals exceeding this age threshold. The extended lifespan is hypothesized to be an adaptation to the extreme seasonality and low metabolic demands of the polar environment, where slow growth rates are balanced by reduced predation pressure and low annual maintenance costs. Comparative analyses with temperate nototheniids suggest that life at sub-zero temperatures may select for a slower pace of life, with delayed reproduction and prolonged somatic persistence. This longevity estimate is critical for parameterizing population models used in the management of Southern Ocean fisheries.

Egg diameter in the blue rockcod ranges from 1.3 to 1.6 mm, and the resulting wet weight at birth is approximately 0.0016 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.0016 grams]. This minute larval size is typical of pelagic-spawning Antarctic fishes that produce numerous small, yolk-laden eggs. Following an incubation period of 140 days [ab = 140 days] at an ambient temperature of -1 °C [T = -1 °C], the embryos hatch as yolk-sac larvae that rely entirely on endogenous reserves before the onset of exogenous feeding. The protracted embryonic phase is a direct consequence of the low thermal regime, which slows metabolic rates and extends all developmental milestones relative to temperate and tropical species. The period from fertilization to eclosion represents a substantial fraction of the first year of life, leaving the prolarvae vulnerable to stochastic environmental fluctuations. Field observations confirm that the timing of hatching is tightly synchronized with the seasonal phytoplankton bloom, ensuring that first-feeding larvae encounter adequate prey concentrations upon transition to exotrophic nutrition.

At an ultimate total length of 30 cm [Li = 30 cm], the maximum adult body mass documented for Indonotothenia cyanobrancha is 660.5 grams [Wwi = 660.5 grams]. This asymptotic size is consistent with the typical body plan of demersal nototheniids that occupy the continental shelf of the Antarctic Peninsula. Growth increment data from tag-recapture studies indicate that individuals approach this maximum mass gradually over the course of their 18-year lifespan, with growth rates decelerating markedly after sexual maturation. The relationship between length and mass in this species follows a cubic scaling function, such that the heaviest specimens are disproportionately large relative to modest increases in linear dimension. Comparative data from congeneric species suggest that this ultimate mass is near the upper end of the range for fish of this body shape, possibly reflecting the energetic advantages of large body size in the cold, viscous waters of the Southern Ocean. The large spawners among the population contribute disproportionately to annual recruitment.

At the persistently low temperature of -1 °C [T = -1 °C] that characterizes the species' habitat throughout the year, the blue rockcod exhibits a maximum fecundity of approximately 25000 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 25000 eggs per spawning event] combined with a single annual spawning event [F_R_i = single annual spawning event]. This high fecundity per event is among the lowest for Antarctic nototheniids in terms of egg size but reflects the high energetic cost of vitellogenesis under extreme thermal conditions. Histological examination of ovarian tissue confirms that oocyte development proceeds slowly but steadily over many months, with group-synchronous maturation ensuring a single, well-timed annual pulse of spawning. The relatively modest fecundity per event is offset by the extended reproductive lifespan of individual females, which may spawn successfully for over a decade. These life-history traits, including a brief post-hatching phase of 140 days [ab = 140 days] at -1 °C [T = -1 °C] prior to the larval transition to external feeding, collectively illustrate an adaptive syndrome shaped by the extreme selective pressures of the polar marine environment.
